claim: The visual system has evolved the ability to track features like color and orientation in parallel.
source: The visual system has evolved the ability to track features like color and orientation in parallel.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about visual system capabilities in the abstract.

claim: The ability to track features in parallel aligns with the specialization of processing these feature dimensions in the visual cortex.
source: This property aligns with the specialization of processing these feature dimensions in the visual cortex.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about cortical organization.

claim: Parallel tracking of changing feature-values within the same feature dimension would have to share the same cortical representation.
source: Parallel tracking would then have to share the same cortical representation, which would set strong limitations on tracking performance.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of cortical organization and its implications.

claim: Sharing the same cortical representation sets strong limitations on tracking performance.
source: Parallel tracking would then have to share the same cortical representation, which would set strong limitations on tracking performance.
evidence: This is an inference about the consequences of shared cortical representation.

claim: Tracking precision is highly imbalanced between streams when tracking two superimposed dot clouds that simultaneously change color along independent trajectories.
source: We find that tracking precision is highly imbalanced between streams and that tracking precision changes over time by alternating between streams at a rate of ~1 Hz.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the reported experiments.

claim: Tracking precision changes over time by alternating between streams at a rate of ~1 Hz.
source: We find that tracking precision is highly imbalanced between streams and that tracking precision changes over time by alternating between streams at a rate of ~1 Hz.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: While parallel color tracking is possible, it is highly limited, essentially allowing for only one color-stream to be tracked with precision at a given time.
source: These observations suggest that, while parallel color tracking is possible, it is highly limited, essentially allowing for only one color-stream to be tracked with precision at a given time.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing imbalanced precision and alternation.

claim: The visual system is proficient in maintaining information about multiple objects at different locations over time.
source: The visual system is very proficient in maintaining information about multiple objects at different locations over time.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: A central processing resource is flexibly distributed amongst multiple relevant locations to explain the ability to maintain information about multiple objects.
source: One common assumption to explain this is a central processing resource that is flexibly distributed amongst multiple relevant locations.
evidence: This is presented as a common theoretical assumption in the field.

claim: Spatial selection mechanisms enable the formation of parallel mental representations of several visual features at distinct locations through visual working memory.
source: Such spatial selection mechanism also enables the formation of parallel mental representations of several visual features at distinct locations through visual working memory (Luck and Vogel, 1997; Scolari et al., 2008; Fukuda et al., 2010; Merkel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Multiple relevant items can be tracked through retinal space over extended periods of time by enhancing the representations of individual spatial locations simultaneously.
source: Furthermore, in a dynamic setting, multiple relevant items can be tracked through retinal space over extended periods of time by enhancing the representations of individual spatial locations simultaneously (Alvarez and Franconeri, 2007; Cavanagh and Alvarez, 2005; Merkel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The distribution of central processing resources amongst relevant locations is internally adjusted by task properties that enhance or reduce interference within the relevant, location-based, domain.
source: The actual distribution of the central processing resource amongst the relevant locations is hereby internally adjusted by task properties that enhance or reduce interference within the relevant, location-based, domain (Shim et al., 2008; Franconeri et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Attentional tracking processes may not solely be tied to visual information traveling through space.
source: Interestingly, it has been suggested that the above-mentioned attentional tracking processes may not solely be tied to visual information traveling through space.
evidence: This is presented as a suggestion from prior research.

claim: A visual object can be tracked through feature-space, in that separate visual features can follow independent trajectories despite them being spatially inseparable.
source: Blaser et al., 2000 showed that a visual object can be tracked through feature-space, in that separate visual features can follow independent trajectories despite them being spatially inseparable.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blaser et al., 2000.

claim: Subjects are able to track an object through a simultaneous change in three separate feature dimensions.
source: In other words, subjects are able to track an object through a simultaneous change in three separate feature dimensions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blaser et al., 2000.

claim: The finding that subjects can track an object through simultaneous changes in three separate feature dimensions supports the notion of object-based attention.
source: This finding supports the notion of object-based attention, according to which attention modulates the processing within all relevant features dimensions the attended object is comprised of Duncan et al., 1997; Schoenfeld et al., 2014.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: According to object-based attention, attention modulates the processing within all relevant features dimensions the attended object is comprised of.
source: This finding supports the notion of object-based attention, according to which attention modulates the processing within all relevant features dimensions the attended object is comprised of Duncan et al., 1997; Schoenfeld et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations.

claim: The visual system may be able to maintain multiple changing feature values within a single feature dimension.
source: Recent data suggests, that the visual system may also be able to maintain multiple changing feature values within a single feature dimension (Re et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Re et al., 2019.

claim: Re et al., 2019 asked subjects to continuously attend two superimposed color dot-motion clouds and detect faint saturation changes in either of them.
source: For example, Re et al., 2019 asked subjects to continuously attend two superimposed color dot-motion clouds and detect faint saturation changes in either of them.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of Re et al., 2019.

claim: The time-course of response accuracies to detect changes of target colors suggests an oscillatory mechanism that allocates feature-based resources sequentially to all relevant items within the feature dimension.
source: The time-course of response accuracies to detect changes of the target colors was taken to suggest an oscillatory mechanism that allocates feature-based resources sequentially to all relevant items within the feature dimension (Re et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation from Re et al., 2019.

claim: Rhythmic sampling of visual information to overcome resource limitations has been discussed extensively as a mechanistic framework for spatial attention.
source: Such rhythmic sampling of visual information to overcome resource limitations has been discussed before extensively as a mechanistic framework for spatial attention (Landau and Fries, 2012; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; VanRullen, 2016), and it has been linked to oscillatory processes measured with electrophysiological recordings (Busch et al., 2009; Song et al., 2014; Landau et al., 2015; Kienitz et al., 2018; Fiebelkorn et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Rhythmic sampling has been linked to oscillatory processes measured with electrophysiological recordings.
source: Such rhythmic sampling of visual information to overcome resource limitations has been discussed before extensively as a mechanistic framework for spatial attention (Landau and Fries, 2012; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013; VanRullen, 2016), and it has been linked to oscillatory processes measured with electrophysiological recordings (Busch et al., 2009; Song et al., 2014; Landau et al., 2015; Kienitz et al., 2018; Fiebelkorn et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Previous research investigating multiple feature tracking asked observers to track constant feature-values to detect target changes in another feature dimension.
source: However, all previous research investigating multiple feature tracking addressed the issue by asking observers to track constant feature-values (e.g. two superimposed colors) to detect target changes in another feature dimension (e.g. a change in luminance or saturation).
evidence: This is a characterization of prior research methods.

claim: Previous forms of feature tracking do not require continuously updating the representation of changing feature-values within the attended streams.
source: Importantly, this form of feature tracking does not require to continuously update the representation of changing feature-values within the attended streams.
evidence: This is an inference about the requirements of previous experimental paradigms.

claim: The question whether feature-based processes are able to maintain representations of multiple changing feature-values within the same dimension remains entirely unresolved.
source: Hence, the question whether feature-based processes are able to maintain representations of multiple changing feature-values within the same dimension, in analogy to multiple-object tracking in space (Alvarez and Franconeri, 2007; Schoenfeld et al., 2014; Pylyshyn, 1989), remains entirely unresolved.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Observers track the color of two superimposed dot clouds that simultaneously move along independent trajectories through color-space in the reported experiments.
source: Specifically, observers track the color of two superimposed dot clouds (Figure 1a) that simultaneously move along independent trajectories through color-space.
evidence: This describes the experimental design used in the current study.

claim: Color-stream specific resource allocation is quantified as the precision of reporting one or both of the tracked colors.
source: Color-stream specific resource allocation is quantified as the precision of reporting one or both of the tracked colors.
evidence: This describes the measurement approach used in the study.

claim: Cognitive resource distribution indexed by the proportion of precision estimates is measured across pairs of simultaneously tracked color-streams in experiments 1 and 2.
source: Cognitive resource distribution indexed by the proportion of precision estimates is measured across pairs of simultaneously tracked color-streams (experiments 1 and 2) and across variable tracking intervals (experiments 3 a-c).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: Cognitive resource distribution indexed by the proportion of precision estimates is measured across variable tracking intervals in experiments 3 a-c.
source: Cognitive resource distribution indexed by the proportion of precision estimates is measured across pairs of simultaneously tracked color-streams (experiments 1 and 2) and across variable tracking intervals (experiments 3 a-c).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach.

claim: In Experiment 1, subjects were asked to simultaneously track the color change of two donut-shaped superimposed dot-clouds.
source: Subjects were asked to simultaneously track the color change of two donut-shaped superimposed dot-clouds as illustrated in Figure 1a.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The calculated trajectories of the two dot-clouds through color space were kept random and unpredictable while never falling below a minimum critical distance.
source: The calculated trajectories of the two dot-clouds through color space were kept random and unpredictable, while never falling below a minimum critical distance, on each experimental trial, and the stimuli were designed in a manner that tracking could not be based on spatial information (c.f. Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes the stimulus design.

claim: The stimuli were designed in a manner that tracking could not be based on spatial information.
source: The calculated trajectories of the two dot-clouds through color space were kept random and unpredictable, while never falling below a minimum critical distance, on each experimental trial, and the stimuli were designed in a manner that tracking could not be based on spatial information (c.f. Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This describes the stimulus design rationale.

claim: Color tracking lasted for 6–8 sec in Experiment 1.
source: Color tracking lasted for 6–8 sec, after which both dot-clouds turned into grey.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: After color tracking, both dot-clouds turned into grey, prompting subjects to report the last perceived color of each stream.
source: Color tracking lasted for 6–8 sec, after which both dot-clouds turned into grey. This prompted subjects to report the last perceived color of each stream (Target a, Target b; before turning grey), by dialing in the color as precisely as possible on a color wheel using a rotary knob (Figure 1b – Exp1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: The precision of the representation for the two color-streams was derived from the two standard deviations of a mixture model of two von Mises distributions containing pairs of target-response distances for all trials.
source: The precision of the representation for the two color-streams (Precision High, Precision Low) was derived from the two standard deviations of a mixture model of two von Mises distributions containing pairs of target-response distances for all trials.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: The target with the smaller of the two possible target-response distances was assigned to response 1 assuming a generally higher confidence for the first given response.
source: On a given trial, the target (a or b) with the smaller of the two possible target-response distances (min(response 1 – target a, response 1 – target b)) was assigned to response 1 assuming a generally higher confidence for the first given response.
evidence: This describes the data analysis assumption.

claim: The absolute precision estimates varied considerably across subjects in Experiment 1.
source: Despite the fact that the resulting absolute precision estimates varied considerably across subjects (range(p1)=9.489, range(p2)=30.995) (Figure 3a), corresponding precision estimates of both streams showed a similar relation across subjects with a correlation of r=0.602 (p=0.008).
evidence: This is supported by the reported statistical results.

claim: Corresponding precision estimates of both streams showed a similar relation across subjects with a correlation of r=0.602 (p=0.008) in Experiment 1.
source: Despite the fact that the resulting absolute precision estimates varied considerably across subjects (range(p1)=9.489, range(p2)=30.995) (Figure 3a), corresponding precision estimates of both streams showed a similar relation across subjects with a correlation of r=0.602 (p=0.008).
evidence: This is supported by the reported statistical results.

claim: A regression model with zero intercept yielded a significant slope of a=1.748 (F(1,17) = 10.588, p=0.0046) in Experiment 1.
source: A regression model with zero intercept (p1=a*p2) yielded a significant slope of a=1.748 (F(1,17) = 10.588, p=0.0046), suggesting an unbalanced resource distribution between the two streams of a similar ratio in each subject, independent of the overall precision of the subject.
evidence: This is supported by the reported statistical results.

claim: The slope of a=1.748 suggests an unbalanced resource distribution between the two streams of a similar ratio in each subject, independent of the overall precision of the subject.
source: A regression model with zero intercept (p1=a*p2) yielded a significant slope of a=1.748 (F(1,17) = 10.588, p=0.0046), suggesting an unbalanced resource distribution between the two streams of a similar ratio in each subject, independent of the overall precision of the subject.
evidence: This is an inference from the statistical results.

claim: None of the pairs of precision estimates were different from a Monte-Carlo simulated set of responses in any of the subjects (p>0.811) in Experiment 1.
source: Importantly, none of the pairs of precision estimates were different from a Monte-Carlo simulated set of responses in any of the subjects (p>0.811), which indicates that the variation in precision between streams arises from independent distributions.
evidence: This is supported by the Monte-Carlo simulation results.

claim: The variation in precision between streams arises from independent distributions.
source: Importantly, none of the pairs of precision estimates were different from a Monte-Carlo simulated set of responses in any of the subjects (p>0.811), which indicates that the variation in precision between streams arises from independent distributions.
evidence: This is an inference from the Monte-Carlo simulation results.

claim: The difference of precision estimates may reflect a recency-based imbalance generated in the response phase rather than an imbalance of resource allocation during color tracking.
source: Accordingly, the difference of precision estimates may not reflect an imbalance of resource allocation during color tracking but a recency-based imbalance generated in the response phase of the experimental trial.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation for the results.

claim: Experiment 2 addresses the possibility of recency effects by having subjects track two color streams but report only one color-stream on a given trial.
source: Experiment 2 addresses this possibility, by having sixteen subjects of experiment 1 track two color streams exactly as in experiment 1, but report only one color-stream on a given trial (Figure 1b – Exp2).
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale.

claim: The precision estimates in Experiment 2 will represent a mixture of distributions.
source: The logic behind this manipulation is that the precision measures of just one color will still sample from both color-streams randomly, but remove the ambiguity of two possible target-response pairings for each trial. The precision estimates will therefore represent a mixture of distributions.
evidence: This is an inference about the expected outcome of the experimental design.

claim: A difference between precision distributions as seen in experiment 1 would verify that the imbalance of resource allocation is truly arising in the color tracking phase.
source: A difference between precision distributions as seen in experiment 1, would verify that the imbalance of resource allocation is truly arising in the color tracking phase.
evidence: This is a prediction about what the results would indicate.

claim: In Experiment 2, the precision measures were subjected to a von Mises mixture model testing two distributions.
source: The precision measures were subjected to a von Mises mixture model testing two distributions.
evidence: This describes the data analysis method.

claim: Monte-Carlo estimates confirm that precision measures in Experiment 2 do not differ from simulated datasets in any of the subjects (p>0.972).
source: Monte-Carlo estimates confirm that they do not differ from simulated datasets in any of the subjects (p>0.972).
evidence: This is supported by the Monte-Carlo simulation results.

claim: The pairs of high and low precision values in Experiment 2 are correlated across subjects (r=0.579, p=0.019).
source: Furthermore, the pairs of high and low precision values are found to be correlated across subjects (r=0.579, p=0.019).
evidence: This is supported by the reported statistical results.

claim: Linear regression with zero intercept in Experiment 2 yielded a significant slope of a=1.928 (F(1,15) = 21.84, p=0.0003).
source: As in experiment 1, the relation between high and low precision estimates was analyzed via linear regression with zero intercept, which yielded a significant slope of a=1.928 (F(1,15) = 21.84, p=0.0003; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is supported by the reported statistical results.

claim: The slope of slightly below 2 in Experiment 2 is similar to the one obtained when testing both color-streams in experiment 1.
source: The slope of slightly below 2 is similar to the one obtained when testing both color-streams in experiment 1, suggesting a robust subject-specific feature-based resource allocation that varies little across tasks.
evidence: This is an inference comparing results across experiments.

claim: The slope of slightly below 2 suggests a robust subject-specific feature-based resource allocation that varies little across tasks.
source: The slope of slightly below 2 is similar to the one obtained when testing both color-streams in experiment 1, suggesting a robust subject-specific feature-based resource allocation that varies little across tasks.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of results across experiments.

claim: With a median of 1.24, less than 5% of the estimated ratios from simulated equal distributions reach a value larger than 1.928.
source: With a median of 1.24 less than 5% of the estimated ratios reach a value larger than 1.928.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The distance between precision estimates in Experiment 1 and 2 was significantly smaller than the distance obtained from random permutations (p=0.0363).
source: The measured distance between experiments was significantly smaller than the distance obtained from random permutations (p=0.0363; Figure 3c), indicating that the ratio of precision estimates is very consistent within the same subjects across experiments.
evidence: This is supported by the permutation test results.

claim: The ratio of precision estimates is very consistent within the same subjects across experiments.
source: The measured distance between experiments was significantly smaller than the distance obtained from random permutations (p=0.0363; Figure 3c), indicating that the ratio of precision estimates is very consistent within the same subjects across experiments.
evidence: This is an inference from the permutation test results.

claim: The ~2:1 ratio of precision estimates for the two color-streams suggests a strongly limited resource that entails a trade-off assignment during tracking.
source: The ~2:1 ratio of precision estimates for the two color-streams suggests a strongly limited resource that entails a trade-off assignment during tracking.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The trade-off allocation could arise because subjects consistently devote more resources to one stream than the other.
source: This could arise because subjects consistently devote more resources to one stream than the other.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: The trade-off allocation could arise because over time the allocation changes in a dynamic fashion randomly or periodically between the attended feature values.
source: Another possibility is that over time the trade-off allocation changes in a dynamic fashion randomly or periodically between the attended feature values.

claim: Experiments 1 and 2 do not allow to distinguish whether subjects consistently devote more resources to one stream or whether allocation changes dynamically over time.
source: Experiments 1 and 2 do not allow to distinguish among these possibilities, because which stream is actually attended at a given moment remains undefined, as we just probe at a random time point after the onset of the color-streams.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Experiments 3 a-c were designed to systematically assess the temporal dynamics of the attentional allocation process among the attended color streams.
source: Experiments 3 a-c were designed to allow us to systematically assess the temporal dynamics of the attentional allocation process among the attended color streams.
evidence: This describes the purpose of Experiments 3 a-c.

claim: At the beginning of half of the trials in Experiment 3, the brightness of one dot group was transiently enhanced to bias subjects to attend this stream first.
source: At the beginning of half of the trials the brightness of one dot group was transiently enhanced (cue-present trials), to bias subjects to attend this stream first and therefore temporally reset any time-varying process involved in resource allocation towards that stream.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: The brightness cue was intended to temporally reset any time-varying process involved in resource allocation towards that stream.
